registered.old: Use reasonable correction cost where supported. Weigh waste, proportionality and whether the breached undertaking was central. Groves favored restoration cost. Peevyhouse used $300 diminution for restoration it treated as incidental. Plante selected repair costs by defect.
registered.new: Start from the loss in value to this owner (§ 347(a)). If that loss is not proved with sufficient certainty, § 348(2) allows damages based on the drop in market price or on the reasonable cost to complete or repair, but cost only if it is not clearly disproportionate to the probable loss in value to the owner. Plante (Wisconsin) allowed repair cost for small defects fixable without unreasonable economic waste, but valued the misplaced wall by diminution, which was zero: moving it ($4,000) would destroy finished work, and it did not affect market price. Groves (Minnesota) gave the reasonable cost of grading wilfully left undone, even above the graded land’s value, treating economic waste as only the wrecking of a completed structure and citing precedent that applies repair cost to remediable defects even after good-faith substantial performance. Peevyhouse (Oklahoma) held that reasonable cost of performance ordinarily governs, but limited the owners to the $300 diminution because both conditions held: the restoration term was merely incidental to the lease’s main purpose, and its economic benefit was grossly disproportionate to its cost.
registered.reason: For Plante's wall the $4,000 relocation cost was proved, yet the court allowed nothing: the wall fell 'clearly under the diminished-value rule' and did not affect market price (C&M 970–971). The node also omitted § 348(2)(b)'s 'not clearly disproportionate' limit, Peevyhouse's two conjunctive conditions (C&M 980–981) and Groves's wilfulness and Snider grounds (C&M 975, 977).

registered.old: Under Algernon Blair’s rule a nonbreaching contractor may recover reasonable value despite a losing deal. If the work in the illustration was worth $55 to supply at reasonable rates, that measure may be $55, with no duplicate recovery and subject to proof.
registered.new: Under Algernon Blair’s rule a nonbreaching contractor that justifiably stopped after part performance may recover reasonable value despite a losing deal. If the work in the illustration was worth $55 to supply at reasonable rates, that measure may be $55, with no duplicate recovery and subject to proof. Restitution is not available to a contractor that has performed all its duties when only a definite sum of money remains due; it recovers the unpaid price, and a full performer cannot recover more than the price (§ 373(2); C&M 992).

Blair contracted to build a naval hospital and subcontracted steel erection and associated equipment to Coastal. Coastal supplied labor and its own cranes. Blair refused to pay crane rental, although the trial court found that the subcontract required payment. After approximately twenty-eight percent of the work, Coastal stopped because of that refusal. Blair finished with another subcontractor.

The trial court calculated approximately $37,000 otherwise due under the subcontract after prior payments, but found that Coastal would have lost more than that amount had it completed the job. Coastal sought the value of the labor and equipment already furnished rather than the profit it would have earned on full contractual performance.

Section 347 measures expectation as (a) the loss in value to the injured party of the other side’s performance, plus (b) any other loss, incidental or consequential, less (c) any cost or other loss avoided by not having to perform. Loss in value is the performance’s value to the injured party himself, not to a hypothetical reasonable person or a market (cmt. b). A builder whose owner repudiates when $60,000 more would finish a $100,000 house recovers $40,000, less any progress payments (Illus. 6). When the seller is injured, the hard part is (c), its cost and loss avoided; when the seller breaches, it is (a), the buyer’s loss in value. Fixed costs, such as a factory, must be borne before any goods can be produced, and the casebook asks how they figure in (c) when lost profits are claimed (C&M 957–958, introducing Vitex).

One court, in Overstreet v. Norden Laboratories (6th Cir.), denied expectation recovery for an ineffective horse vaccine because no effective vaccine was available from anyone, treating the point as causation; a dissenting judge called this an “alternative product” rule. In contrast, the Chatlos Systems v. NCR (3d Cir.) majority accepted the buyer’s evidence of the value of a computer system that would perform as NCR warranted, rejecting NCR’s argument that valuing it far above the price paid was like substituting a Rolls-Royce for a Ford (C&M 967–968).

Section 348 supplies alternatives when loss in value cannot be proved with sufficient certainty. If a breach delays the use of property, damages may rest on its rental value or on interest on its value (§ 348(1)). If a promise is conditioned on a fortuitous event and it is uncertain whether the event would have occurred, damages may rest on the value of the conditional right, such as a one-in-four chance at a $100,000 prize worth $25,000; this applies only to aleatory promises, so a repudiated contractor must still prove it could and would have performed (§ 348(3), cmt. d, Illus. 5). Subsection (2) governs defective or unfinished construction (see completion damages).

On a losing contract the injured party may recover expenditures made in preparation for performance or in performance, less any loss that the party in breach proves with reasonable certainty the injured party would have suffered had the contract been performed (§ 349). Learned Hand in L. Albert & Son v. Armstrong Rubber put that burden on the party in breach because by its wrong it made the issue relevant, so reliance recovery stops at what performance would have yielded only when the loss is proved (C&M 988). The Security Stove problem asks about trade-show expenses incurred when the profits from exhibiting could not be shown (C&M 992).

After the other party’s total breach or repudiation, § 373(1) gives the injured party restitution for any benefit conferred by part performance or reliance, and Algernon Blair measured it without deducting the loss the claimant would have suffered on completion, “undiminished by any loss which would have been incurred by complete performance” (C&M 991). The casebook opens the topic with a lottery buyer whose ticket was never delivered and who could “get his money back whether or not he eventually would have won,” asks whether an injured party is therefore generally entitled to restitution under a losing contract, and offers Learned Hand’s reduce-by-proven-loss rule for reliance as a possible solution (C&M 988). The Flour Markets problem asks whether a buyer that prepaid $500,000 of a $1,400,000 price may recover it from a seller that failed to deliver after the market fell to $1,100,000 (citing Bush v. Canfield, C&M 989). A party that has fully performed and is owed only a definite sum of money has no restitution claim (§ 373(2)).

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Plante v. Jacobs: This case separates three questions: whether performance is substantial, which defects are compensable, and how each defect should be valued. It links the conditions doctrine in Jacob & Youngs to the competing damages measures in Groves and Peevyhouse. The problems that follow ask whether loss in value, cost to remedy or the builder’s savings should control when a defect causes no market loss: a pool built shallower than promised that would cost $180,000 to rebuild (Ruxley), 14 guards supplied instead of 20 for a meeting no protester attended, and defective bird feeders that $600 would repair after the market price fell (UCC § 2-714(1)) (C&M 972–973).

Groves v. John Wunder Co.: Groves makes the promised physical result central to expectation damages. Peevyhouse later adopts a different treatment of a similarly disproportionate restoration obligation.

Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.: Peevyhouse connects contractual purpose and bargaining evidence to the measure of damages. Its facts show why a complete remedies analysis must distinguish market value, personal value, and the performance expressly purchased. The casebook asks what Restatement § 348(2) would do in both cases (C&M 981): if the owner cannot prove his own loss in value with sufficient certainty, cost is unavailable when clearly disproportionate to the probable loss in value, so cost above $60,000 for land worth $12,160 when graded, or about $29,000 for a $300 increase, would likely yield diminution unless the owner proved the work worth more to him than its market effect. The editors ask whether the Peevyhouses’ loss in value might have been the jury’s $5,000.

United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.: This case separates restitution from both expectation and reliance. It is especially useful when a plaintiff has partly performed a contract that would have lost money.

Star Paving problem (C&M 968): Drennan wrongfully stopped Star when finishing would have cost Star $5,000 on a $15,000 subcontract, and Star at once contracted with the School District to finish the same work for $7,000. Under Restatement § 347 cmt. d, the net profit from a substitute arrangement using the freed resources is subtracted unless the injured party could and would have had both contracts (“lost volume,” cmt. f). Because Star could not have done the same job twice, its $2,000 profit appears to reduce its damages from $10,000 to $8,000, even though builders are generally assumed to have lost volume when they take new jobs (C&M 967), subject to the casebook’s question whether different terms in the second contract would matter.

Paradox problem (C&M 988): to justify recovery for breach of a contract on which neither party appears to have relied, a court reasons that the injured party might have passed up a similar alternative contract but need not prove it; then, in calculating damages, it reasons that the injured party lost volume because it would have made both contracts. The problem asks how to reconcile the two assumptions before the losing-contracts material.

International notes (C&M 954): CISG article 46(1) lets a buyer require the seller’s performance, but article 28 frees a court from ordering specific performance unless it would do so under its own law for similar sales, which in the United States means UCC § 2-716(1) (Magellan); the casebook asks what is wrong with a remedy that depends on the forum. UNIDROIT Principles article 7.2.2 allows performance of a non-money obligation to be required unless the obligee can reasonably obtain it from another source. Posner traces the civil-law preference for specific performance to canon law, though differences in outcome are said to be small.

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullOld:
The majority distinguished Groves by characterizing the main transaction as a mining arrangement rather than a contract whose principal object was grading or construction. It also drew on authorities comparing completion costs with the benefit to be obtained. Although restoration would not require demolishing a completed building, the majority considered the disproportion between expenditure and economic benefit sufficient under its chosen formulation.

This reasoning makes characterization decisive: calling restoration incidental narrows the protected expectation even though the clause was expressly included. The dissent’s account of bargaining shows the difficulty of equating an improvement’s market value with the owners’ contractual interest. The holding therefore belongs beside the contrary Groves approach and the narrower destructive-repair reasoning in Plante and Jacob & Youngs.

new.label: Award the owner’s damages
new.detail: The owner recovers the loss in value fixed under the test for choosing a measure, plus any incidental or consequential loss, less any cost it avoided (§ 347). Groves reversed a market-value judgment and ordered a new trial at the reasonable cost of the grading Wunder wilfully left undone, first deciding what the grading covenant actually required (C&M 977–978). Peevyhouse reduced the judgment to the $300 diminution in value (C&M 981).
